name: Temple of the Tooth
label: Temple of the Tooth
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kandy View Point' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kandy View' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191377765: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic' (21 m across).
notes: Sacred Buddhist temple housing the tooth relic and Kandy's top sight.

text.description:
The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa) is the Buddhist temple in Kandy that holds the tooth relic of the Buddha. It stands in the old Royal Palace Complex and is part of a World Heritage Site. The temple you see today was built under Vira Narendra Sinha. The octagonal Paththirippuwa and the moat came later, in the reign of Sri Vikrama Rajasinha. The Kandy Esala Perahera is held every year to pay homage to the Sacred Tooth Relic.

The best all-round photo is from above, not at the gates. Guides call it the classic postcard view. The viewpoint is free and open to the public. The temple is small in the frame, so take one wide shot for the setting and one zoomed-in shot for the temple itself.

If you want a different angle, walk the lakeside path at Kandy Lake. From there the white roofs and spires are reflected in the water, and you stand at ground level. Photography is restricted inside the temple, so plan on exterior pictures. Take a few shots with people in them if you can, as they show the scale of the place.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in the centre of Kandy, in the former Royal Palace Complex beside Kandy Lake. The viewpoint is on the hillside to the south-east, on Rajapihilla Mawatha, looking down over the city.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Start from the Temple of the Tooth beside Kandy Lake in the city centre. The viewpoint is to the south-east and uphill, on Rajapihilla Mawatha. It is about 25 minutes on foot. Once you are on the hillside platform, the temple lies to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the wide view of lake, hills and rooftops. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the temple. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people crowd the platform and you want to step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kandy View Point (built platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, uphill above the city). Kandy Lake, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and surrounding green hills in one panoramic frame, with the temple among the rooftops below. From here the temple sits to the north-west among the rooftops, with Kandy Lake and the green hills around it in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top third line, so the lake and rooftops fill the lower part of the frame. Then take a second, zoomed shot with the temple roofs on a third line. If the platform is busy, the lakeside walk at Kandy Lake gives a different view, with the spires reflected in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the roofs are not too bright. At dusk, try night mode and rest your elbows on a solid ledge or wall, if there is one, to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or just before sunset, when crowds are smaller and the light is softer. At sunset you may also catch the city lights coming on.

text.access_note: Kandy View Point is a free public platform, but check the official site before you go for opening hours and festival-day restrictions. The temple itself is a place of worship, where shoulders and knees must be covered and photography is restricted inside.

name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya
label: Peradeniya Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Royal Palm Avenue' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Palmyra Palm Avenue' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6776379: large area 'Triangle' (1645 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large botanic garden with orchids, palm avenues and giant trees.

text.description:
Royal Palm Avenue is the classic postcard view of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya. Tall royal palms stand in two straight rows and seem to meet in the distance, so the avenue works as a natural leading line. It is a very easy picture to take on a phone: the symmetry does most of the work for you.

The gardens cover 147 acres beside the Mahaweli River and hold more than 4,000 species of plants, including orchids, spices, medicinal plants and many kinds of palm. The garden was formally established in 1843, and the avenues along River Drive are among its best-known features. Elsewhere in the grounds you can find the Cannonball Tree planted by King George V and Queen Mary in 1901.

Walk to the entrance end of the avenue and shoot down its length. Keep yourself in the middle of the path so both rows of palms look evenly balanced. Wait for a gap in the walkers if you can, or let one or two people stand in the distance to show how tall the trees are. Other good spots nearby are the Suspension Bridge, for river and bank views, and the Great Lawn, where the giant Java fig spreads over the grass. The gardens are a big site, so wear comfortable shoes and allow plenty of time.
text.geographic_location: The gardens are at Peradeniya, about 5.5 km west of Kandy city, close to the Mahaweli River. Royal Palm Avenue is one of the avenues along River Drive inside the grounds.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so travel about 5.5 km west of Kandy to Peradeniya. Once inside, follow River Drive to Royal Palm Avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot down the avenue. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the palms to look even taller, but keep the phone level so the rows don't lean. The telephoto (2x or more) squeezes the palms closer together, which can look striking from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Royal Palm Avenue (main palm avenue, shoot down the length of the avenue from the entrance end). A symmetrical view of tall royal palms converging along a straight path, with the avenue as a leading line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the middle of the path on the centre line, so both rows of palms mirror each other. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level. A portrait (upright) frame suits the tall trunks, and a landscape frame shows more of the path. If you want a different view, the Suspension Bridge frames the river and its banks, and the Great Lawn shows the full spread of the giant fig.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the avenue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take a few frames, as walkers will change the picture from one second to the next.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The light along the avenue is best in the first hour after the gardens open, when the path is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The gardens are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for entry details and any closures.

name: Queen's Hotel, Kandy
label: Queen's Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kandy View Point' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kandy View' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/966305223: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Queen's Hotel' (77 m across).
notes: Colonial-era hotel facing the lake and the temple.

text.description:
Queen's Hotel is a 90-room British Colonial style hotel at the end of Kandy's main street, and it is one of the oldest hotels in Sri Lanka, with more than 160 years of history. The building began as a royal residence, the Dullawe Walauwa, built for King Sri Wickrama Rajasinha. After the British defeated the Kandyan Kingdom in 1815 it became a mansion for the Governor of Ceylon. Later it served as barracks, then a hostel and boarding house, and it took the name Queens Hotel in 1869.

It is an elevated terrace with a wide view over the town, where the hotel sits alongside Kandy Lake and the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic. From here the hotel is one part of a bigger scene, not a close-up, so think of it as a town portrait with the hotel as one landmark in it. If you want the building's frontage itself, D S Senanayake Veediya, formerly Malabar Street, is the alternative. Keep your phone steady against a railing or wall, and wipe the lens first, as hazy hill air and fingerprints soften distant shots quickly.
text.geographic_location: Queen's Hotel is in the centre of Kandy, at the end of the main street, close to Kandy Lake and the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic. The viewpoint is on higher ground to the south-east of the centre, looking back over the town.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so you will need your own way to reach Kandy View Point from the middle of Kandy. Once you are on the terrace, the hotel lies to the north-west, about 1.7 km away in a straight line. For the street view, head for D S Senanayake Veediya in the town centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick the hotel out of the town. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) or panorama for the whole scene, and the default lens (1x) for a balanced frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kandy View Point. An elevated panorama in which Queen's Hotel appears alongside Kandy Lake, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and the town. If you want the hotel's frontage and the temple area nearby, walk to D S Senanayake Veediya instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the hotel on a third line, with the lake and temple area filling the rest of the frame. Take one wide shot first for the scene, then zoom in for a second frame where the hotel is the main subject. In the second frame, keep the horizon level. For a variation, take a panorama and sweep slowly from the lake across to the hotel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hotel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. If you use zoom above 2x, brace your elbows on the rail and take two or three frames, then keep the sharpest. Switch on night mode for the lights after dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Reviewers say the view is especially good around sunset, when the city lights come on. Arrive a little before, so you can try your frames while the light is still soft.

text.access_note: Kandy View Point appears to be free to enter, but check on the day. The hotel is a working business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or photograph from its grounds.

name: Ceylon Tea Museum
label: Ceylon Tea Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3276843504: the OpenStreetMap point 'Ceylon Tea Museum'.
notes: Old tea factory on the hill with tea-making exhibits and views.

text.description: The Ceylon Tea Museum fills a former tea factory about 3 km south of Kandy. The Hanthana Tea Factory was built in 1925, and the four-storey building has plenty of character for a photo: the tall, plain factory shape is the main subject, and the old machinery inside gives you close-up detail pictures. The area around Hanthana was one of the first to grow tea successfully after coffee failed in Sri Lanka. The factory stood abandoned for more than a decade before it was refurbished and opened as a museum on 1 December 2001. Inside, the ground floor holds 19th-century colonial generators, rollers, dryers, fermentation tables and sorting machines, so there are lots of textures and metal shapes to look at. Higher up there is a library and museum floor, then a shop, and a restaurant and tea rooms at the top. Exhibits also cover tea pioneers such as James Taylor and Thomas Lipton. For your phone, start outside and take one wide shot to show how tall the building is. Then go indoors for details: a roller, a dryer door, a row of old sorting machines. Move slowly and keep the phone steady, because indoor light can be dim. Check the official site before you go to find out what is open and whether photography is allowed in every area.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Hanthana area, about 3 km south of the centre of Kandy, in the former Hanthana Tea Factory.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Kandy and head south for about 3 km. Ask for the Ceylon Tea Museum at Hanthana, and check the official site before you go in case access details have changed. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) outside to fit the tall four-storey building into one frame. Indoors, use the default lens (1x) for machines and rooms, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as dials, rollers and labels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your wide shot from the open ground outside, as far back as is comfortable, and keep the whole factory in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building straight, so the walls do not lean inward. Outside, include the full height of the factory. Indoors, look for repeating shapes, such as rows of machines or the wheels and belts of old equipment, and fill the frame with them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the machinery to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright windows wash out the picture. If a room is dim, hold the phone steady against a wall or rail and let night mode work if it switches on. Keep portrait mode for people, not machines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the museum is open and quieter, so you can take your time indoors. Outside, soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the building than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: This is a museum with a shop and restaurant, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and photography rules.

name: Kandy railway station
label: Kandy Railway Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kandy Railway Station' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/258496237: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kandy' (140 m across).
notes: Colonial-era station, the end of the famous hill-country train line.

text.description: Kandy railway station is the town's main station and one of the most significant in the central hills. It makes a good photo stop because two quite different styles sit side by side. The station building is Art Moderne, with curving forms and long horizontal lines. Behind it, the roof over the platforms is older Victorian work, with arches and fine metalwork. The front of the building, with its clock tower and arched windows, is the main shot here. The station also has a real railway history. The first steam engine reached Kandy on 16 April 1867, and the first passenger service began on 1 August 1867. The station stands about 512 m above sea level, 120 km from Colombo, which helps explain why trains here feel like part of the hill-country journey. For the classic railway picture, wait on the platform for a train to arrive or leave, with the arches and platform architecture behind it. Stay behind the safety line the whole time. Inside, the arched roof makes a good frame, and a few seconds spent looking along the platform often gives a cleaner picture than the first angle you try. Go early in the morning if you can, when there are fewer people in the frame. Photographing the building and trains for your own use is generally accepted, but check with Sri Lanka Railways before any professional or commercial shoot.
text.geographic_location: In the town of Kandy, on the site known as Deiyange Wela. The station sits on a branch of the Main Line that leads on to the Matale Line.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground-style stops are listed for this spot, so start from the middle of Kandy and go by taxi or hired scooter. The station is the town's main railway station, so drivers should know it. The phone icon on the map marks the station itself, in the middle of the building, so you are at the spot as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the arched platform roof, and use 2x-3x telephoto for details such as the clock and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the full front facade, step back to the forecourt or the road in front so the whole building is in view. Alternatively, use the platform for a train arriving or leaving with the station architecture behind it, always staying behind the safety line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the building up square on, so the vertical walls and the clock tower stay straight. Include the arched windows and keep a little space around the roofline. For the second shot, put the train on one side of the frame and let the platform arches lead the eye along the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo when a train pulls in, so you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when there are fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a working railway station, so photograph from public areas, stay behind the platform safety line, and check with Sri Lanka Railways before any professional or commercial shoot.

name: Royal Palace of Kandy
label: Royal Palace of Kandy
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kandy View Point' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kandy View' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191377766: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Royal Palace' (72 m across).
notes: Former palace of the Kandyan kings next to the Temple of the Tooth.

text.description:
The Royal Palace of Kandy was the official home of the Kandyan kings until British rule began in 1815. What remains is a cluster of historic buildings beside the Temple of the Tooth, including the Royal Audience Hall (Magul Maduwa), whose construction began in 1783, and the King's Palace, now a museum. The palace has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, and was rebuilt in 1634 under Rajasinha II. Only a handful of its structures survive, so expect a few carved buildings and courtyards rather than one grand palace. The complex is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

For the best phone photo of the whole scene, use Kandy View Point, a viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha above the city. From here you get a wide panorama of Kandy Lake, the Temple of the Tooth and the old palace area, with green hills behind. The palace itself is small and distant from this height, so treat it as part of a cityscape, not the main subject. If you want close detail of the carved walls and the courtyard with the temple beyond, walk down to the palace itself later. Photography rules differ between the palace buildings and the temple, so check the signs at each entrance. Photography is banned in the temple's inner sanctum, and dress should cover shoulders and knees.
text.geographic_location: The palace sits in the heart of Kandy, in the old royal quarter beside the Temple of the Tooth and Kandy Lake. Kandy View Point is on Rajapihilla Mawatha, on higher ground to the south-east, looking back over the city.
text.directions_text: Coming back down, the palace area lies to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full sweep of lake, temple and hills. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the palace roofs and the temple beside it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and hillside.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kandy View Point (viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, above the city). A wide panorama of Kandy Lake, the Temple of the Tooth and the old royal palace area, with green hills behind. From here the old royal palace area lies to the north-west, close to the temple and the edge of Kandy Lake, with green hills behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the lake on the lower third, with the temple and palace area just above it. Include some of the railing or a tree at the edge to give depth. For a closer, more detailed shot, walk down to the palace courtyard, where the carved walls can be framed with the Temple of the Tooth beyond. The Royal Palace Park is another option for garden scenes with flower beds and trees, but it may not give a clear view of the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lake or the temple to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. For the wide view, try panorama mode and pan slowly. At dusk, night mode works if you rest your arms on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the light is softest and the city lights come on.

text.access_note: Kandy View Point is a public viewing platform, but check the official site before you go to the palace buildings and the Temple of the Tooth, as entry and photography rules apply there.
claims_not_in_sources: The palace is small and distant in the view from Kandy View Point, so a telephoto lens (2x-5x) helps to pick it out.
Resting your arms on a railing helps keep the phone steady for night mode.

name: Kandy Clock Tower
label: Kandy Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sri Dalada Veediya / S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha junction' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Sri Dalada Veediya and S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q16830485: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Landmark clock tower in the city centre.

text.description:
The Kandy Clock Tower stands right in the middle of the city, on the junction of Sri Dalada Veediya, S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha and Hiragedara Mawatha. It was built in 1950 by Haji Mohamed Ismail as a monument to his son, Mohamed Zacky Ismail, who died in a landslide accident at Kadugannawa in 1947. The clock machinery was brought over from the United Kingdom, and the tower was completed on 23 December 1950, though it was not officially opened until the following year. The architect was Shirley de Alwis. He drew on the Kandyan style and worked in elements of the Temple of the Tooth and the king's palace.

It photographs well because it is a tall, clear shape set against a lively street. From the corner you can fit the whole tower in with the traffic and pedestrians around its base, which tells you more about Kandy than a close-up of the clock face would. The junction is very busy, and one visitor review notes there is nowhere to sit nearby, so plan to take your photos quickly and keep an eye on the traffic. Stand on the pavement, not in the road, and let people pass. Give yourself a minute to check the frame before you press the shutter, because the scene changes constantly. A second option is to wait for the tower to stand against the hills and the setting sun, with street life below.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Kandy, on the junction where Sri Dalada Veediya, S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha and Hiragedara Mawatha meet, close to the Ismail Building.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Kandy and ask for the Clock Tower at the junction of Sri Dalada Veediya and S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha. The tower is on the junction itself, so you cannot miss it once you are there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and the busy junction around it. Then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the tower alone. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the clock face and the carved details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Sri Dalada Veediya and S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha (the street junction at the tower's base, where Hiragedara Mawatha also meets). A wider street-level view of the tower framed by the busy intersection, traffic and pedestrians. From here you see the whole structure framed by the intersection, the traffic and the people crossing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright and level, so the tower's sides stay straight instead of leaning. Leave some street at the bottom of the frame to include the traffic and pedestrians. If you would like the tower against the hills and a setting sun, try that as a second shot instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the tower is not a silhouette. Live Photos can catch passing traffic and people for a lively street moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset, when the sun and hills can sit behind the tower. Early morning is likely to be quieter on the street.

text.access_note: The tower stands on a public street junction and can be photographed from the pavement; it is very busy with traffic and pedestrians, so take care.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the street than later in the day.
Standing on the pavement at the junction is safer than standing in the road.
A bright sky can make the tower look dark in a phone photo unless the exposure is lowered.
The tower and hills can be seen together near sunset.

name: Malwathu Maha Viharaya
label: Malwathu Maha Vihara
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sangaraja Mawatha' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sangaraja Mawatha nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1837320502: the OpenStreetMap point 'Malwathu Maha Viharaya'.
notes: Major Buddhist monastery of the Siyam Nikaya.

text.description:
Malwathu Maha Viharaya, also called Malwatta Temple, is a working Buddhist monastery and the headquarters of the Malwatta Chapter of the Siyam Nikaya. It is one of two monasteries that share the custodianship of the sacred tooth relic kept at the Sri Dalada Maligawa, so it has a long and important place in Kandy's religious life. It is believed to have been founded by Senasammatha Vikramabahu in the late 15th or early 16th century. The oldest part, the Poyamalu Viharaya, is an archaeologically protected monument. The assembly hall known as the 'poya ge' dates from the reign of Kirti Sri Rajasinha.

For a phone photo, the best approach is from the lakeside, not from inside the grounds. That gives you a calm, layered picture: water, shoreline, then rooftops and trees. The Temple of the Tooth and the Udawattekele forest can also be seen from the same stretch, so it is worth turning around to look. Kandy Lake itself is a good second option, where the monastery is seen across the water from the lake bank. Keep your photos respectful: this is a living monastery, so photograph the buildings from outside and ask before taking pictures of any monks.
text.geographic_location: Malwathu Maha Viharaya stands in central Kandy, on the shore of Kandy Lake, close to the Temple of the Tooth. The photo spot is on Sangaraja Mawatha, where the road meets the lake promenade.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed nearby, so start from central Kandy, around the Kandy Lake and Temple of the Tooth area, and walk to Sangaraja Mawatha at the lakeside. The monastery is just south of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the monastery, the shore and the lake together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rooftops and trees across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sangaraja Mawatha (lakeside, at the point where the road meets the Kandy Lake promenade, looking toward the monastery). The Malwatta monastery buildings rising above the shore of Kandy Lake, with the lake in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the shoreline on the lower third line, so the lake fills the foreground and the monastery sits above it. Keep the horizon level. Try a second shot at 2x or 3x to isolate the buildings. For a different view, walk along the lake bank and photograph the monastery across the water, using the lake as a reflecting foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monastery buildings to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls and roofs keep their detail. If the water is still, wait for the ripples to settle before you press the shutter. Live Photos can catch a little movement on the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits lake views best. Midday sun can make the water glare, so lower the exposure slider if you are there then.

text.access_note: The monastery is an active place of worship, so ask locally before you go about visiting inside; the lakeside viewpoint is on a public road and promenade.

name: Asgiri Maha Viharaya
label: Asgiri Maha Vihara
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Asgiri Maha Viharaya' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4036017572: the OpenStreetMap point 'Asgiri Maha Viharaya'.
notes: Historic temple with a large reclining Buddha.

text.description:
Asgiri Maha Viharaya is a Buddhist monastery on the north side of Kandy Lake. It is the headquarters of the Asgiriya Chapter of the Siyam Nikaya, one of the two monastic chapters that look after the sacred tooth relic kept at the Temple of the Tooth. For a phone photographer, the draw is the white pagoda in the foreground, with the surrounding hills and village rooftops stretching out behind it. Walking the path around the pagoda gives you that landscape as a backdrop from several angles, and the temple also looks striking from the road below.

The monastery was founded by Commander Siriwardhana on the instructions of King Parakramabahu IV, who reigned from 1305 to 1335. It is made up of several temples, including the middle temple (Meda Pansala), built in 1767, and the new temple (Aluth Viharaya), built a year later. The grounds also hold a 36-foot recumbent Buddha carved from rock, and the old royal cremation ground of the Kandyan kings.

Take your time on the path and look for a clear gap between the pagoda and the hills, so the white stupa stands out against the greenery. Photography is generally fine outdoors and around the stupa, but not inside the shrine halls or during worship. Dress modestly and be ready to remove your shoes in sacred areas. If you want to photograph monks, ask first and be respectful.
text.geographic_location: Asgiri Maha Viharaya stands on the north side of Kandy Lake, in the Asgiriya area of Kandy. It sits on higher ground above the town, with views out over the hills.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stop is close by. The monastery lies north of Kandy Lake, so head north from the lake to reach it. The site is on a hillside, so expect an uphill approach on foot at the end. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the pagoda and the hills behind it into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the pagoda itself. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out village rooftops and ridgelines in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the white pagoda is in the foreground, with the mountains and village rooftops behind it, looking out over the hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pagoda on one of the vertical lines, leaving the hills and rooftops to fill the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. Walk a few steps around the path to move the pagoda against a different part of the view. Please stay outside the shrine halls when taking photos, and keep monks out of the shot unless they have agreed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stays bright and detailed rather than washed out. Use panorama (held steady, moving slowly) for the sweep of hills if you want a wider scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white pagoda. Avoid the harsh middle of the day if you can, as the bright white surfaces can overexpose.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and expect to remove your shoes in sacred areas; photography is restricted inside shrine halls and during worship, and you should check current opening hours before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than the middle of the day.
Bright white surfaces can overexpose in strong midday sun on a phone camera.

name: St. Paul's Church, Kandy
label: St. Paul's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deva Veediya' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Deva Veediya nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/191377762: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Paul's Church' (60 m across).
notes: Anglican church from 1843 near the temple.

text.description: St. Paul's is an Anglican church in the old part of Kandy, just west of the Temple of the Tooth. Its red-brick Neo-Gothic front is a calm change from the busier sights nearby, and the warm brick colour shows up well on a phone. The church was built mainly from solid terracotta bricks. The foundation stone was laid on 16 March 1843, and it was consecrated on 25 January 1853. Because British officials and the garrison first used it, it is also called the Garrison Church. Inside is the only pipe organ in Kandy. A similar-sized organ from a closed church in Bradford replaced the original in 2009. From the street in front of the entrance you get the full façade, with the Temple of the Tooth area close by. For the best result, stand back far enough to fit the whole front in the frame and keep the building upright by using the gridlines. If you want something quieter, the side of the church shows the brickwork and window bays. The churchyard, with its banyan tree and old graves, gives a greener picture, but check on arrival that it is open to visitors. Photography inside is restricted, so keep to the exterior. The church holds services, so do not block the entrance, and ask permission if staff or worshippers are nearby.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Kandy, on Deva Veediya (number 10), just west of the Temple of the Tooth.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Temple of the Tooth area in the centre of Kandy. The church is just to the west of the temple. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the church. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement or road keeps you too close, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brickwork and window details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Deva Veediya (directly in front of the church entrance, on the road side). The red-brick Neo-Gothic façade of the church, framed from the street with the Temple of the Tooth area nearby. Keep clear of the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the walls and the façade so the building does not lean. Keep a little street in the foreground to give a sense of place. For an alternative, try the side view of the south wall with its brickwork and window bays, or the churchyard view with the banyan tree and old graves if the grounds are open to visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. If you use 0.5x, stay square on to the building to limit stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick and fewer people on the street. Avoid service times, such as Saturday prayers, when the entrance needs to stay clear.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship; photography inside is restricted and the rules for the grounds are unclear, so shoot from the street and check the official site or ask on the spot before going in.

name: Kandy Lake
label: Kandy Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kandy View Point' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kandy View Garden Road' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5966035: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Artificial lake beside the temple with a walking path all around.

text.description:
Kandy Lake is the calm, man-made centrepiece of the hill city, and it is what makes Kandy look the way it does in photographs. King Sri Wickrama Rajasinghe had it made in 1807 next to the Temple of the Tooth, turning old paddy fields into water. The shoreline has a low, white scalloped wall known as the Clouds Wall. It runs for roughly 630 metres, and its triangular openings were once used for oil lamps on festival days. A small island in the middle carries an old pavilion. The whole lake is about 3.2 km around.

The lake photographs best from above. From there the lake sits in the middle distance, with the temple, the rooftops below and the green hills around the city. Guides often call this the classic postcard view of Kandy. At lake level, the path around the water gives you shady, close-up pictures of the wall and the island instead.

For your phone, treat the water as the middle layer of the picture, with sky and hills above and the town below. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. The platform has limited room and can be busy around sunset, so arrive a little early to claim a good spot on the platform. Roadside parking gets congested at busy times, so allow extra time if you come by car.
text.geographic_location: Kandy Lake lies in the centre of Kandy, right beside the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and the town's main streets.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Kandy, beside the lake and the Temple of the Tooth. The viewing platform is on Rajapihilla Mawatha, on the hill to the south-west of the lake, so you head uphill in that direction. It is roughly 2 km from the lake and the walk is steep. A short tuk-tuk ride is the easier option. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view, with the lake, the temple and the hills all in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit it all in or want a wider panorama. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the temple roofs and the island pavilion.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kandy View Point (viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, above the lake and city). The lake in the middle distance, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, the rooftops below and the green hills around the city, often with the single chair in the frame. Face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line so the lake and the rooftops fill most of the frame. Keep the water in the middle of the picture, with the temple area to one side and hills along the top. If you want a closer shot, zoom in on the island and the pale wall along the shore. A second option is the lakeside spot at Kandy Lake View Point, where the lake appears at water level with the temple and hills behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lake or the hills to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour. As the city lights come on at dusk, try night mode and rest your elbows on a steady surface to keep the phone steady. For a sweeping view, use panorama mode and sweep slowly from left to right.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is the favourite, when the city lights start to come on. Sunrise is also recommended.

text.access_note: Several guides describe Kandy View Point as a free public platform, but the lakeside path may close during festivals or ceremonies, so check locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A telephoto zoom can pick out the island pavilion and temple roofs from the viewpoint.
Dropping the exposure slider helps keep colour in the sky at dusk.

name: Helga's Folly
label: Helga's Folly
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Helga's Folly' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q106433118: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Eccentric hilltop hotel with colourful, fantasy interiors.

text.description:
Helga's Folly is an Art Nouveau boutique hotel on a hillside in Kandy, and the building itself is the photograph. It began as the family home, designed by Esme de Silva in the 1930s. In the mid-1990s her daughter, Helga de Silva Blow Perera, inherited it and gave it the name it has today. The hotel calls itself an 'anti-hotel' and is filled with antiques, murals and family photographs. That odd, crowded character is what makes the front of the building so much fun to shoot.

From the phone icon on the map, you are at the front of the building, where the drive climbs up from Rajaphilla Mawatha. The hillside frontage, the drive leading up to it and the jungle and lake-side setting behind all fit into one frame. That gives your photo a real sense of place rather than just a close-up of a wall.

The building is a hotel and restaurant, so it is private property. Ask at reception before you start photographing. Keep your shots to the front. The rear is reported to have been damaged in a recent cyclone, so avoid framing that side. Early evening is a good time to visit because the light is soft and kind to the colours.
text.geographic_location: Helga's Folly is on a hillside above Kandy, reached from Rajaphilla Mawatha (the hotel's address is 70 Rajaphilla Mawatha). It sits on a hillside with jungle and a lake-side setting behind it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so ask for Helga's Folly on Rajaphilla Mawatha or use the hotel's address (70 Rajaphilla Mawatha, Kandy) to navigate. Once there, walk up the drive to the front of the building, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the drive and the building won't fit in one frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as murals and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are right at the subject, so the building fills the view and the hillside and greenery sit behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the drive as a leading line towards the front of the building. Keep the jungle and the lake-side setting behind it in the frame. Keep your phone level so the walls don't lean, and leave out the rear of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the building's front, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky is washing out the sky and walls. Check the result before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when the light is soft.

text.access_note: The building is a private hotel and restaurant, so ask at reception before photographing.

name: Udawattakele Forest Reserve
label: Udawattakele Forest
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kodimale' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kodimale Peak' (node/3416295417): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7876953: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Forest reserve above the lake with walking trails and monkeys.

text.description:
Udawattakele is a 104-hectare forest on a hill ridge right in the city of Kandy. In the days of the Kandyan kings it was the "garden above the royal palace" and was kept for the royal family, which is why it was once called the Forbidden Forest. It became a forest reserve in 1856 and a sanctuary in 1938. Today it is known for its birds and its giant lianas, among many plant species.

For photographs, the best spot is the summit of the reserve's highest peak, known as Flag Point or Kodimale. The ridge top stands 635 metres above sea level, about 115 metres above Kandy Lake. From here you can glimpse the city and the lake through the forest canopy. The foliage filters the view, so you will find gaps and frames rather than one wide open panorama. Treat the leaves as part of the picture and let the city show through behind them.

If you have time, two other places inside the reserve suit phone photos. The Royal Pond (Kiri Muhuda), the old royal bathing pond, gives a calm, tree-framed reflection. Pus Wela, a very old giant liana winding up through the trees, makes a good tall forest-detail shot.

The climb to the summit is on a hill trail. Paths can be slippery after rain, and leeches can be a nuisance in wet weather, so wear shoes with a good grip.
text.geographic_location: Udawattakele lies on a hill ridge in the city of Kandy, stretching from the Temple of the Tooth towards the Uplands and Aruppola housing areas, above Kandy Lake.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Temple of the Tooth in central Kandy and go to the visitors' entrance on the western side of the forest, beside Tapovanaya Monastery. On foot, the entrance is about 15 to 20 minutes from the Temple of the Tooth, going north and then uphill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the city and lake glimpsed through the trees. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the forest canopy and trail. Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the lake or rooftops through a gap in the leaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (summit of the reserve's highest peak (Flag Point), reached by the Kodimale trail). Kandy city and lake glimpsed through the forest canopy from the highest point of the reserve.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Look for a gap in the foliage and let the leaves frame the city and lake rather than hiding them. Switch on gridlines and place the lake or skyline on a lower line. If you come down to the Royal Pond, try a still-water shot with the trees around it. For Pus Wela, hold the phone upright and shoot up along the liana.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the distant city, not the nearby leaves, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the view. Under the trees, use night mode only if the light is very dim, and hold the phone still against your body or a tree.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend morning (about 7 to 10 AM) or late afternoon.

text.access_note: This is a forest reserve with an entry fee, at least for foreign visitors, and trail conditions can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Natha Devale, Kandy
label: Natha Devale
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6968771: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Oldest surviving building of the Kandyan royal complex.

text.description:
Natha Devale is a historic shrine standing on the terrace in front of the Royal Palace complex in Kandy. Tradition says it was already here before the Tooth Relic arrived in the city, and it is thought to be the oldest surviving building in Kandy, believed to have been built by King Vikramabahu III in the 14th century. The name Natha means 'lord' or 'protector', and locally the deity is usually linked with Maitreya, the future Buddha.

It photographs well because it gives you real age and a sense of place in one frame: an old shrine set against the palace terrace. In the days of the Kandyan kings, royal names were given here, and in the annual Esala Perahera the Natha Devale procession follows straight after the Dalada Perahera. The Vishnu Devale lies to the north, inside the inner palace complex, so you may notice other shrines close by.

Take that first, then zoom in for details such as the roofline and doorway. Keep the phone level using the gridlines so the building does not lean. Be quiet and respectful, as this is a shrine, and avoid photographing worshippers close-up without asking.
text.geographic_location: Natha Devale is in central Kandy, on the terrace in front of the Royal Palace complex. The Vishnu Devale lies just to the north, within the inner palace complex.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Royal Palace complex area in central Kandy. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the shrine in its setting. Then switch to telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x if your phone has it) for roof and doorway details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step much closer and want the whole building in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front facade, from the raised stone terrace facing the Temple of the Tooth). The shrine's tiled, layered roof and carved front, framed against the open terrace in front of the Royal Palace complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the shrine on one of the vertical lines, with the terrace in the lower third of the picture. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls stay straight. Take one wide shot with the palace complex behind, then a closer zoomed shot of the roof and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the shrine's walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not turn dark. Avoid digital zoom beyond your phone's telephoto lens, as the picture gets soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more even light. Check the dates of the Esala Perahera if you want to see the procession, but expect it to be crowded.

text.access_note: This is a shrine and a place of worship, so dress modestly and behave respectfully. Check locally before you go for any access rules or restrictions.
